english: The lights are on if and only if someone is home. The lights aren't on, so nobody's home.
note: 'Nobody's home' is the negation of 'someone is home'

english: The alarm goes off exactly when the door is opened. The alarm went off, so the door was opened.
note: Valid only because it's a biconditional, as a plain conditional this would affirm the consequent

english: The match goes ahead if and only if the rain stops. The rain hasn't stopped, so the match won't go ahead.
We'll have the picnic unless it rains. It's not raining, so we're having the picnic.
I'll be on time unless the train is delayed. I wasn't on time, so the train must have been delayed.
note: 'A unless B' written as A∨B here, to check scoring accepts either form

english: I can't borrow books unless I have a library card. I don't have one, so I can't borrow any books.
note: A is the negative 'I can't borrow books', so ¬B→A is ¬Y→¬X

english: Either Jake or Priya will pick you up from the airport. Jake can't make it, so Priya will.
The coin landed on either heads or tails, but not both. It didn't land on heads, so it landed on tails.
Exactly one of Ben and Chloe is lying. Ben isn't lying, so Chloe is.
I'm ordering either the cake or the ice cream, but not both. I'm ordering the cake, so I'm not getting the ice cream.
note: Affirming a disjunct is valid for exclusive or, compare 'affirming-disjunct-battery'

english: Neither Alex nor Sam came to the party. So Sam didn't come.
If it's a weekday, either the bakery or the café is open. Neither the bakery nor the café is open, so it isn't a weekday.
I won't take both the Sydney job and the Perth job. I'm taking the Sydney one, so I won't take the Perth one.
It's sunny but freezing. So it's freezing.
I slept nine hours, yet I'm still tired. If I'm tired, I'm skipping the gym. So I'm skipping the gym.
note: 'Still tired' and 'tired' are the same claim

english: Although Leo trained every day, he lost the race. If Leo lost the race, he won't make the team. So he won't make the team.
